title: From the chain rule to network timestep certificates
before: The next reading preserves the original line-by-line dissipation, discrete-step and network-geometry arguments. after: The shared mathematical bridge is the chain rule, not a universal controller. For the active quadratic use its declared Hessian; for a random-affordable actor there is no reason to substitute the historical flux law. A certificate that controls numerical overshoot also does not prove that an action is physically permitted.

title: Preservation, routes and the distinction between invariance and attraction
before: These original chapters retain the full preservation certificate, route and Bellman discussion, and long-run distinctions. Their reserve, uncertainty, regeneration and threshold symbols are historical assumptions, not additional fields silently added to the Gaussian world. after: Keep three conclusions separate: a certificate may protect one declared source boundary; a planner may find a beneficial route; and a process may or may not recover. None implies the others. The next laboratory returns to fixed Gaussian references and lossless finite quantities, without importing this reading's regenerative plant.

title: The original P1C permission layer
before: This source reading explains the original classifier and source-budget mechanism in full. It is retained because reusing its arithmetic without its source-typing premises previously obscured the difference between preservation and internal transfer. Its prohibition for finite extraction is not adopted here as a general prohibition on moving the conserved scalar.
after: Reuse of proportional scaling does not adopt the permission policy that supplies its budget. An implementation must choose and authorize the latter explicitly. We can now discuss event order without allowing a convenient helper to define the plant in secret.

title: One historical synchronous tick, slowly
before: The original walkthrough makes frozen evaluation and synchronous execution concrete. Its natural-drive and P1C chronology are not the proposed forcing-first Gaussian chronology. Compare the order of operations, not just the spelling of variables.
after: Two event profiles can contain the same-looking operations and still implement different models. The prospective profile must specify when forcing is applied, when state is frozen and which accepted increment is valued. Reordering an implementation is not an editorial amendment.

title: The original exact-quote implementation

title: From a historical quote to its receipt
before: The original receipt and settlement discussion is preserved with its original scientific scope. Publication-era references to a receipt do not grant the new programme an owner map or a persistent spendable-capacity policy. Read the records as a sequence of distinct commitments, observations and checks.
after: The Gaussian proposal adds a prospective persistent account, not merely a new name for an old receipt. Therefore its owner mapping, signed updates and atomic publication need their own authority. An exact field difference is still not a wage or an entitlement.

title: Original tests and their failure targets
before: The original chapter gives concrete examples of what a test is meant to catch. Counts and pass statements refer only to that historical implementation and its recorded configuration. No test count is transferred to a Gaussian runtime.
after: The enduring lesson is to make plausible mistakes detectable. The current book's arithmetic checks test teaching examples, not runtime acceptance. A future transition test must be classified as a transition even if its fixture is small.

title: Reproducing evidence without rewriting it
before: This full historical reproduction chapter preserves the original record structure and its caution about reinterpreting outcomes. Commands and paths inside the reading document that edition; they are not instructions to execute them now or launch a later study.
after: Reproducibility requires the actual scientific packet and operational permission, not a copied command. Historical bytes remain inspectable while corrections and later findings are recorded separately. This distinction also explains why old experimental pages are retained rather than silently edited into new results.

after: We now have the necessary historical vocabulary for the evidence sequence: the plant, controller, permission and measurement layers are identified. title: O14 and a flat outcome
before: This reading preserves the original destination-choice account, including its limitations and flat result. It predates the later finalized Gate 1D-C record discussed above. Do not combine its run counts or conclusions with that later campaign.
after: A flat result is informative only relative to a design capable of detecting the proposed difference. Preserve the original observation, distinguish implementation conformance from efficacy, and ask whether the metric and world discriminate the competing claims. This does not license tuning a frozen study after its results.

title: What a field account must actually observe
before: The original measurement chapter develops the practical difference between a mathematical coordinate and an observed physical quantity. Its examples remain scoped to their own plant. New loss carriers or new calibration rules require new declarations rather than the relabelling of an old sensor field.
after: A hash authenticates a record's bytes, not the truth of a reading. The Gaussian potential still requires credible stocks, references and scales. With that distinction in place, the final chapters can state what long-run research would need to establish without claiming those results already exist.
